# Cantor space

- [Deutsch](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor-Raum)
- [Español](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espacio_de_Cantor)
- [Français](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espace_de_Cantor)
- [Italiano](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spazio_di_Cantor)
- [日本語](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%82%AB%E3%83%B3%E3%83%88%E3%83%BC%E3%83%AB%E7%A9%BA%E9%96%93)
- [Nederlands](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor-ruimte)
- [中文](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%BA%B7%E6%89%98%E5%B0%94%E7%A9%BA%E9%97%B4)
 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q616653#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Topological space

In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), a **Cantor space**, named for [Georg Cantor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Cantor), is a [topological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) abstraction of the classical [Cantor set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_set): a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) is a Cantor space if it is [homeomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphic) to the Cantor set. In [set theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_theory), the topological space 2ω is called "the" Cantor space.

## Examples

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=1)]

The [Cantor set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_set) itself is a Cantor space. But the canonical example of a Cantor space is the [countably infinite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countably_infinite) [topological product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_topology) of the [discrete 2-point space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_2-point_space) {0, 1}. This is usually written as      2   N      {\displaystyle 2^{\mathbb {N} }}   or 2ω (where 2 denotes the 2-element [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) {0,1} with the [discrete topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_topology)). A point in 2ω is an infinite binary sequence, that is a sequence that assumes only the values 0 or 1. Given such a sequence *a*0, *a*1, *a*2,..., one can map it to the [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number)

∑  n = 0   ∞      2  a  n     3  n + 1     .   {\displaystyle \sum _{n=0}^{\infty }{\frac {2a_{n}}{3^{n+1}}}.}

This mapping gives a homeomorphism from 2ω onto the Cantor set, demonstrating that 2ω is indeed a Cantor space.

Cantor spaces occur abundantly in [real analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_analysis). For example, they exist as [subspaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subspace_topology) in every [perfect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_set), [complete metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_metric_space). (To see this, note that in such a space, any [non-empty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empty_set) perfect set contains two [disjoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjoint_sets) non-empty perfect subsets of arbitrarily small diameter, and so one can imitate the construction of the usual [Cantor set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_set).) Also, every [uncountable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncountable), [separable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separable_space), [completely metrizable space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completely_metrizable_space) contains Cantor spaces as subspaces. This includes most of the common spaces in real analysis.

## Characterization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=2)]

A topological characterization of Cantor spaces is given by [Brouwer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luitzen_Egbertus_Jan_Brouwer)'s theorem:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-1)

**Brouwer's theorem**—Any two non-empty [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space) [Hausdorff spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_space) without [isolated points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isolated_point) and having countable [bases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_(topology)) consisting of [clopen sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clopen_set) are homeomorphic to each other.

The topological property of having a base consisting of clopen sets is sometimes known as "[zero-dimensionality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-dimensional)". Brouwer's theorem can be restated as:

**Theorem**—A [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) is a Cantor space [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) it is non-empty, [perfect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_set), [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space), [totally disconnected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totally_disconnected), and [metrizable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metrizable).

This theorem is also equivalent (via [Stone's representation theorem for Boolean algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone's_representation_theorem_for_Boolean_algebras)) to the fact that any two [countable atomless Boolean algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countable_atomless_Boolean_algebra) are [isomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphic).

Without metrizability, the statement fails. A [Cantor cube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_cube)      2  α     {\displaystyle 2^{\alpha }}  , for     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }   an uncountable ordinal, is not homeomorphic to the Cantor space (and thus is not metrizable).

## Properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=3)]

As can be expected from Brouwer's theorem, Cantor spaces appear in several forms. But many properties of Cantor spaces can be established using 2ω, because its construction as a product makes it amenable to analysis.

Cantor spaces have the following properties:

- The [cardinality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinality) of any Cantor space is      2   ℵ  0       {\displaystyle 2^{\aleph _{0}}}  , that is, the [cardinality of the continuum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinality_of_the_continuum).
- The product of two (or even any finite or countable number of) Cantor spaces is a Cantor space. Along with the [Cantor function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_function), this fact can be used to construct [space-filling curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space-filling_curve).
- A (non-empty) Hausdorff topological space is compact metrizable if and only if it is a [continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function_(topology)) [image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_(mathematics)) of a Cantor space.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-4)

Let *C*(*X*) denote the space of all real-valued, [bounded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_function) continuous [functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) on a topological space *X*. Let *K* denote a compact [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space), and Δ denote the Cantor set. Then the Cantor set has the following property:

- *C*(*K*) is [isometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isometry) to a [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_set) subspace of *C*(Δ).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-5)

In general, this isometry is not unique, and thus is not properly a [universal property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_property) in the [categorical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_theory) sense.

- The [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) of all homeomorphisms of the Cantor space is [simple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_group).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-6)

## Cantor group

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=4)]

The Cantor space becomes an [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group)     { 0 , 1  }   Z      {\displaystyle \{0,1\}^{\mathbb {Z} }}   where the group operation is defined as pointwise addition [modulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo) 2. Thus if     (  x  i    )  i ∈  Z      {\displaystyle (x_{i})_{i\in \mathbb {Z} }}   and     (  y  i    )  i ∈  Z      {\displaystyle (y_{i})_{i\in \mathbb {Z} }}   are two points of the Cantor space, with      x  i   ,  y  i   ∈ { 0 , 1 }   {\displaystyle x_{i},y_{i}\in \{0,1\}}  , the group law is given by     (  x  i   ) + (  y  i   ) = (  x  i   +  y  i    mod  2   ) .   {\displaystyle (x_{i})+(y_{i})=(x_{i}+y_{i}{\bmod {2}}).}   The identity element is the constant sequence      x  i   = 0   {\displaystyle x_{i}=0}  . Since     x + x ≡ 0   ( mod  2 )    {\displaystyle x+x\equiv 0{\pmod {2}}}   for any     x ∈ { 0 , 1 }   {\displaystyle x\in \{0,1\}}  , every element of the group is an [involution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Involution_(mathematics)), i.e.,     (  x  i   ) + (  x  i   ) = ( 0  )  i ∈  Z      {\displaystyle (x_{i})+(x_{i})=(0)_{i\in \mathbb {Z} }}   or, equivalently, the inverse element of     (  x  i   )   {\displaystyle (x_{i})}   is     (  x  i   )   {\displaystyle (x_{i})}   itself, i.e.,     − (  x  i   ) = (  x  i   )   {\displaystyle -(x_{i})=(x_{i})}  .

The Cantor group is a compact abelian [topological group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group), making it an important example in [abstract harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_harmonic_analysis). Every continuous [character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_(mathematics)) on the Cantor group Every continuous character of     G = { 0 , 1  }   Z      {\displaystyle G=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb {Z} }}   has the form      χ  F   ( x ) = ( − 1  )   ∑  i ∈ F    x  i     ,   {\displaystyle \chi _{F}(x)=(-1)^{\sum _{i\in F}x_{i}},}   where     F ⊂  Z    {\displaystyle F\subset \mathbb {Z} }   is finite. Thus the [Pontryagin dual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_dual) is naturally identified with the group of finite subsets of      Z    {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} }  , under [symmetric difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_difference), or equivalently with      ⨁   Z     Z   /  2  Z    {\displaystyle \bigoplus _{\mathbb {Z} }\mathbb {Z} /2\mathbb {Z} }   under addition. This can be identified with the additive group of        G ^    =   F   2   [  t  − 1   , t ]   {\displaystyle {\widehat {G}}=\mathbb {F} _{2}[t^{-1},t]}   of [Laurent polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_polynomial) over the [field with two elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_with_two_elements). Here     t   {\displaystyle t}   corresponds to the character      χ  1   ( x ) = ( − 1  )   x  1     .   {\displaystyle \chi _{1}(x)=(-1)^{x_{1}}.}   This group is sometimes known as the *Walsh group* in this context.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-SchippWadePal-7)

A particularly important group of [automorphisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphism) of the Cantor group are the [shift maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shift_map)      s  n   (  x  i   ) = (  x  i + n   )   {\displaystyle s_{n}(x_{i})=(x_{i+n})}   for     n   {\displaystyle n}   an integer. The effect of      s  n     {\displaystyle s_{n}}   is to shift the sequence to the left     n   {\displaystyle n}   units (if     n > 0   {\displaystyle n>0}  ) or to the right by      |  n  |    {\displaystyle |n|}   units (if     n < 0   {\displaystyle n<0}  ). The mapping     n ↦  s  n     {\displaystyle n\mapsto s_{n}}   is a representation of the additive group of integers      Z    {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} }   into the autormorphism group of     G   {\displaystyle G}  . On characters, the shift action is     χ (  s  n   x ) =  t  n   χ ( x )   {\displaystyle \chi (s_{n}x)=t^{n}\chi (x)}  .

The [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure) on the Cantor group is the [probability measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_measure) that assigns each coordinate      x  i     {\displaystyle x_{i}}   an equal probability     1  /  2   {\displaystyle 1/2}   of coming up     0   {\displaystyle 0}   or     1   {\displaystyle 1}  . Equivalently, the measure assigned to a cylinder set     X = { (  x  i   )  |   x   i  1     =  a  1   ,  x   i  2     =  a  2   , … ,  x   i  k     =  a  k   }   {\displaystyle X=\{(x_{i})|x_{i_{1}}=a_{1},x_{i_{2}}=a_{2},\dots ,x_{i_{k}}=a_{k}\}}  , where the indices      i  j     {\displaystyle i_{j}}   are distinct, is      2  − k     {\displaystyle 2^{-k}}  .

The Cantor space      2   N      {\displaystyle 2^{\mathbb {N} }}   maps to the [unit interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_interval), by the map     (  x  i    )  i ∈  N    ↦  ∑  n = 0   ∞      x  n    2  n + 1       {\displaystyle (x_{i})_{i\in \mathbb {N} }\mapsto \sum _{n=0}^{\infty }{\frac {x_{n}}{2^{n+1}}}}  . Under this map, the [pushforward measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pushforward_measure) of the Haar measure is the [Lebesgue measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_measure), and the Walsh characters define the [Rademacher functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher_function). This view is useful in the [harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis).

The Cantor group is a protypical example of a [profinite group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profinite_group). It is the [inverse limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_limit) of the groups      F  2   n     {\displaystyle F_{2}^{n}}   under the coordinate projection maps      F  2   n + 1   →  F  2   n     {\displaystyle F_{2}^{n+1}\to F_{2}^{n}}  . Topologically, every profinite group is homeomorphic to the Cantor space, but need not be isomorphic to it. An example is the additive group       Z   2     {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} _{2}}   of [2-adic integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2-adic_integers). This is an inverse limit of the groups      Z   /   2  n    Z    {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} /2^{n}\mathbb {Z} }   under the reduction maps      Z   /   2  n + 1    →    mod  2    n      Z   /   2  n    Z    {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} /2^{n+1}\xrightarrow {{\bmod {2}}^{n}} \mathbb {Z} /2^{n}\mathbb {Z} }  , but is not isomorphic to it as a group. For example,       Z   2     {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} _{2}}   contains no nontrivial involutions. More generally, the additive group of the [p-adic integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_integers) is homeomorphic to the Cantor space (as is the [ring of integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_integers) in any non-archimedean [local field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_field)).

## Topology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=5)]

The [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) of the Cantor space can be specified by giving the [basic open sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_open_set). Given a finite sequence      a  1   , … ,  a  n   ∈ { 0 , 1 }   {\displaystyle a_{1},\dots ,a_{n}\in \{0,1\}}  , the [cylinder set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cylinder_set)     U (  a  1   , … ,  a  n   ) = { (  x  i   )  |   x  1   =  a  1   , … ,  x  n   =  a  n   }   {\displaystyle U(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n})=\{(x_{i})|x_{1}=a_{1},\dots ,x_{n}=a_{n}\}}   is an open set. It is also a closed set, its complement being the union of open sets     U (  a  1  ′  ,  a  k  ′  , … ,  a  n  ′  )   {\displaystyle U(a'_{1},a'_{k},\dots ,a'_{n})}   where at least one      a  i  ′    {\displaystyle a_{i}'}   is different from      a  i     {\displaystyle a_{i}}  . Thus it is a [clopen set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clopen_set). Not every open subset of the Cantor space is clopen, but this basis of the topology consists entirely of clopen sets, a general feature of profinite spaces.

This basis of the topology can be described as follows.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-Kitchens-8) If     F   {\displaystyle F}   is a finite subset of      N    {\displaystyle \mathbb {N} }  , then there is a projection      π  F   : { 0 , 1  }   N    → { 0 , 1  }  F     {\displaystyle \pi _{F}:\{0,1\}^{\mathbb {N} }\to \{0,1\}^{F}}   corresponding to restricting the coordinates to     F   {\displaystyle F}  . Now,     { 0 , 1  }  F     {\displaystyle \{0,1\}^{F}}   is a finite set, and it can be given the [discrete topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_topology). The topology on the Cantor space is the coarsest topology making all of the maps      π  F     {\displaystyle \pi _{F}}   continuous; i.e., it is the [initial topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_topology) of the family of projections. The basic open sets are thus stratified into        U    F   = {  π  F   − 1   ( S )  |  S ⊂ { 0 , 1  }  F   } .   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {U}}_{F}=\{\pi _{F}^{-1}(S)|S\subset \{0,1\}^{F}\}.}   The topology on the Cantor space is generated by      ⋃  F ⊂  N  ,   |  F  |  < ∞      U    F     {\displaystyle \bigcup _{F\subset \mathbb {N} ,\,|F|<\infty }{\mathcal {U}}_{F}}  , by closing this under the unions of elements.

### Continuous functions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=6)]

A function on the Cantor space is continuous if, for every     ϵ > 0   {\displaystyle \epsilon >0}   there is a finite set     F   {\displaystyle F}   of integers such that      |  f ( x ) − f ( y )  |  < ϵ   {\displaystyle |f(x)-f(y)|<\epsilon }   for all     x   {\displaystyle x}   and     y   {\displaystyle y}   that agree on     F   {\displaystyle F}  .

### Locally constant functions and distributions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=7)]

A particular subspace of the space of continuous functions is the [locally constant functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_constant_function). A function is locally constant if there is a partition of the Cantor space into clopen subsets, such that the function is constant on each set of the partition. Let      C  l c   ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C_{lc}(\Delta )}   denote the space of locally constant functions on the Cantor space     Δ   {\displaystyle \Delta }  . The space      C  l c   ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C_{lc}(\Delta )}   carries a finer topology than     C ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C(\Delta )}   by declaring that a sequence      f  n   → 0   {\displaystyle f_{n}\to 0}   if any only if all but finitely many      f  n     {\displaystyle f_{n}}   agree outside a finite set of     F   {\displaystyle F}   of coordinates, and converge on the residual finite-dimensional space of functions on     { 0 , 1  }  F     {\displaystyle \{0,1\}^{F}}  . This stronger topology is a [nuclear topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_space) defining a space of [test functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_function) and whose [continuous dual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_dual) defines a space of [distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_(mathematics)).

## Banach algebras

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=8)]

Several natural commutative [Banach algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebra) are associated with the Cantor space (or group)     Δ   {\displaystyle \Delta }  . The Banach algebra     C ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C(\Delta )}   under pointwise multiplication, with the [supremum norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supremum_norm), is the most fundamental. It has the property that the [Gelfand spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_spectrum) is     Δ   {\displaystyle \Delta }   itself, and the Gelfand embedding     C ( Δ ) → C (  Δ  ∨   )   {\displaystyle C(\Delta )\to C(\Delta ^{\vee })}   is an isomorphism (and is canonical). This is typical of [Stone spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_space), but not of other [compact Hausdorff spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Hausdorff_space).

On the Cantor group, another Banach algebra is the [group algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_algebra_of_a_locally_compact_group), which is the space      L  1   ( Δ , μ )   {\displaystyle L^{1}(\Delta ,\mu )}   of      L  1     {\displaystyle L^{1}}  -integrable classes of functions on     Δ   {\displaystyle \Delta }   with respect to the Haar measure     μ   {\displaystyle \mu }  , and the [convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolution) operation as multiplication:     ( f ∗ g ) ( t ) =  ∫  Δ   f ( t − x ) g ( x )  d x .   {\displaystyle (f*g)(t)=\int _{\Delta }f(t-x)g(x)\,dx.}   The maximal ideal space is the Pontryan dual        Δ ^    =  ⨁   Z     Z   /  2  Z    {\displaystyle {\widehat {\Delta }}=\bigoplus _{\mathbb {Z} }\mathbb {Z} /2\mathbb {Z} }  . The Gelfand transform is the Fourier transform, associating to     f ∈  L  1   ( Δ , μ )   {\displaystyle f\in L^{1}(\Delta ,\mu )}   the function        f ^    ( γ )   {\displaystyle {\hat {f}}(\gamma )}   of a character     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }   given by        f ^    ( γ ) =  ∫  Δ   f ( x ) γ ( x )  d x   {\displaystyle {\hat {f}}(\gamma )=\int _{\Delta }f(x)\gamma (x)\,dx}   (there is no [complex conjugate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_conjugate) in the characters, because the characters are all real.)

Likewise, the algebra      ℓ  1   (    Δ ^    )   {\displaystyle \ell ^{1}({\widehat {\Delta }})}   of absolutely summable functions on the countable [discrete group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_group)        Δ ^      {\displaystyle {\widehat {\Delta }}}   is a group algebra under the group convolution. Then     Δ   {\displaystyle \Delta }   is the space of maximal ideals in      ℓ  1   (    Δ ^    )   {\displaystyle \ell ^{1}({\widehat {\Delta }})}  , and the Fourier transform is a one-to-one map from      ℓ  1   (    Δ ^    )   {\displaystyle \ell ^{1}({\widehat {\Delta }})}   onto a subalgebra of     C ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C(\Delta )}  , the [Wiener algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener_algebra). The Wiener algebra     A ( Δ )   {\displaystyle A(\Delta )}   includes all of the locally constant functions, but is a proper subset of     C ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C(\Delta )}  :      C  l c   ( Δ ) ⊂ A ( Δ ) ⊂ C ( Δ ) .   {\displaystyle C_{lc}(\Delta )\subset A(\Delta )\subset C(\Delta ).}

Cantor space

# Cantor space

- [Deutsch](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor-Raum)
- [Español](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espacio_de_Cantor)

In [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), a **Cantor space**, named for [Georg Cantor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Cantor), is a [topological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) abstraction of the classical [Cantor set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_set): a [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) is a Cantor space if it is [homeomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeomorphic) to the Cantor set. In [set theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_theory), the topological space 2ω is called "the" Cantor space.

Examples

# Examples

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=1)]

The [Cantor set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_set) itself is a Cantor space. But the canonical example of a Cantor space is the [countably infinite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countably_infinite) [topological product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_topology) of the [discrete 2-point space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_2-point_space) {0, 1}. This is usually written as      2   N      {\displaystyle 2^{\mathbb {N} }}   or 2ω (where 2 denotes the 2-element [set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics)) {0,1} with the [discrete topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_topology)). A point in 2ω is an infinite binary sequence, that is a sequence that assumes only the values 0 or 1. Given such a sequence *a*0, *a*1, *a*2,..., one can map it to the [real number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number)

∑  n = 0   ∞      2  a  n     3  n + 1     .   {\displaystyle \sum _{n=0}^{\infty }{\frac {2a_{n}}{3^{n+1}}}.}

This mapping gives a homeomorphism from 2ω onto the Cantor set, demonstrating that 2ω is indeed a Cantor space.

Cantor spaces occur abundantly in [real analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_analysis). For example, they exist as [subspaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subspace_topology) in every [perfect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_set), [complete metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_metric_space). (To see this, note that in such a space, any [non-empty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empty_set) perfect set contains two [disjoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjoint_sets) non-empty perfect subsets of arbitrarily small diameter, and so one can imitate the construction of the usual [Cantor set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_set).) Also, every [uncountable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncountable), [separable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separable_space), [completely metrizable space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completely_metrizable_space) contains Cantor spaces as subspaces. This includes most of the common spaces in real analysis.

Characterization

# Characterization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=2)]

A topological characterization of Cantor spaces is given by [Brouwer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luitzen_Egbertus_Jan_Brouwer)'s theorem:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-1)

**Brouwer's theorem**—Any two non-empty [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space) [Hausdorff spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_space) without [isolated points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isolated_point) and having countable [bases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_(topology)) consisting of [clopen sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clopen_set) are homeomorphic to each other.

The topological property of having a base consisting of clopen sets is sometimes known as "[zero-dimensionality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-dimensional)". Brouwer's theorem can be restated as:

**Theorem**—A [topological space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) is a Cantor space [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) it is non-empty, [perfect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_set), [compact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_space), [totally disconnected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totally_disconnected), and [metrizable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metrizable).

This theorem is also equivalent (via [Stone's representation theorem for Boolean algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone's_representation_theorem_for_Boolean_algebras)) to the fact that any two [countable atomless Boolean algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countable_atomless_Boolean_algebra) are [isomorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isomorphic).

Without metrizability, the statement fails. A [Cantor cube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_cube)      2  α     {\displaystyle 2^{\alpha }}  , for     α   {\displaystyle \alpha }   an uncountable ordinal, is not homeomorphic to the Cantor space (and thus is not metrizable).

Properties

# Properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=3)]

As can be expected from Brouwer's theorem, Cantor spaces appear in several forms. But many properties of Cantor spaces can be established using 2ω, because its construction as a product makes it amenable to analysis.

Cantor spaces have the following properties:

- The [cardinality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinality) of any Cantor space is      2   ℵ  0       {\displaystyle 2^{\aleph _{0}}}  , that is, the [cardinality of the continuum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinality_of_the_continuum).
- The product of two (or even any finite or countable number of) Cantor spaces is a Cantor space. Along with the [Cantor function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_function), this fact can be used to construct [space-filling curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space-filling_curve).
- A (non-empty) Hausdorff topological space is compact metrizable if and only if it is a [continuous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function_(topology)) [image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_(mathematics)) of a Cantor space.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-4)

Let *C*(*X*) denote the space of all real-valued, [bounded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_function) continuous [functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_(mathematics)) on a topological space *X*. Let *K* denote a compact [metric space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space), and Δ denote the Cantor set. Then the Cantor set has the following property:

- *C*(*K*) is [isometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isometry) to a [closed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_set) subspace of *C*(Δ).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-5)

In general, this isometry is not unique, and thus is not properly a [universal property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_property) in the [categorical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_theory) sense.

- The [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_(mathematics)) of all homeomorphisms of the Cantor space is [simple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_group).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-6)

Cantor group

# Cantor group

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=4)]

The Cantor space becomes an [abelian group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abelian_group)     { 0 , 1  }   Z      {\displaystyle \{0,1\}^{\mathbb {Z} }}   where the group operation is defined as pointwise addition [modulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo) 2. Thus if     (  x  i    )  i ∈  Z      {\displaystyle (x_{i})_{i\in \mathbb {Z} }}   and     (  y  i    )  i ∈  Z      {\displaystyle (y_{i})_{i\in \mathbb {Z} }}   are two points of the Cantor space, with      x  i   ,  y  i   ∈ { 0 , 1 }   {\displaystyle x_{i},y_{i}\in \{0,1\}}  , the group law is given by     (  x  i   ) + (  y  i   ) = (  x  i   +  y  i    mod  2   ) .   {\displaystyle (x_{i})+(y_{i})=(x_{i}+y_{i}{\bmod {2}}).}   The identity element is the constant sequence      x  i   = 0   {\displaystyle x_{i}=0}  . Since     x + x ≡ 0   ( mod  2 )    {\displaystyle x+x\equiv 0{\pmod {2}}}   for any     x ∈ { 0 , 1 }   {\displaystyle x\in \{0,1\}}  , every element of the group is an [involution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Involution_(mathematics)), i.e.,     (  x  i   ) + (  x  i   ) = ( 0  )  i ∈  Z      {\displaystyle (x_{i})+(x_{i})=(0)_{i\in \mathbb {Z} }}   or, equivalently, the inverse element of     (  x  i   )   {\displaystyle (x_{i})}   is     (  x  i   )   {\displaystyle (x_{i})}   itself, i.e.,     − (  x  i   ) = (  x  i   )   {\displaystyle -(x_{i})=(x_{i})}  .

The Cantor group is a compact abelian [topological group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_group), making it an important example in [abstract harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_harmonic_analysis). Every continuous [character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_(mathematics)) on the Cantor group Every continuous character of     G = { 0 , 1  }   Z      {\displaystyle G=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb {Z} }}   has the form      χ  F   ( x ) = ( − 1  )   ∑  i ∈ F    x  i     ,   {\displaystyle \chi _{F}(x)=(-1)^{\sum _{i\in F}x_{i}},}   where     F ⊂  Z    {\displaystyle F\subset \mathbb {Z} }   is finite. Thus the [Pontryagin dual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontryagin_dual) is naturally identified with the group of finite subsets of      Z    {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} }  , under [symmetric difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_difference), or equivalently with      ⨁   Z     Z   /  2  Z    {\displaystyle \bigoplus _{\mathbb {Z} }\mathbb {Z} /2\mathbb {Z} }   under addition. This can be identified with the additive group of        G ^    =   F   2   [  t  − 1   , t ]   {\displaystyle {\widehat {G}}=\mathbb {F} _{2}[t^{-1},t]}   of [Laurent polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_polynomial) over the [field with two elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_with_two_elements). Here     t   {\displaystyle t}   corresponds to the character      χ  1   ( x ) = ( − 1  )   x  1     .   {\displaystyle \chi _{1}(x)=(-1)^{x_{1}}.}   This group is sometimes known as the *Walsh group* in this context.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-SchippWadePal-7)

A particularly important group of [automorphisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphism) of the Cantor group are the [shift maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shift_map)      s  n   (  x  i   ) = (  x  i + n   )   {\displaystyle s_{n}(x_{i})=(x_{i+n})}   for     n   {\displaystyle n}   an integer. The effect of      s  n     {\displaystyle s_{n}}   is to shift the sequence to the left     n   {\displaystyle n}   units (if     n > 0   {\displaystyle n>0}  ) or to the right by      |  n  |    {\displaystyle |n|}   units (if     n < 0   {\displaystyle n<0}  ). The mapping     n ↦  s  n     {\displaystyle n\mapsto s_{n}}   is a representation of the additive group of integers      Z    {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} }   into the autormorphism group of     G   {\displaystyle G}  . On characters, the shift action is     χ (  s  n   x ) =  t  n   χ ( x )   {\displaystyle \chi (s_{n}x)=t^{n}\chi (x)}  .

The [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure) on the Cantor group is the [probability measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_measure) that assigns each coordinate      x  i     {\displaystyle x_{i}}   an equal probability     1  /  2   {\displaystyle 1/2}   of coming up     0   {\displaystyle 0}   or     1   {\displaystyle 1}  . Equivalently, the measure assigned to a cylinder set     X = { (  x  i   )  |   x   i  1     =  a  1   ,  x   i  2     =  a  2   , … ,  x   i  k     =  a  k   }   {\displaystyle X=\{(x_{i})|x_{i_{1}}=a_{1},x_{i_{2}}=a_{2},\dots ,x_{i_{k}}=a_{k}\}}  , where the indices      i  j     {\displaystyle i_{j}}   are distinct, is      2  − k     {\displaystyle 2^{-k}}  .

The Cantor space      2   N      {\displaystyle 2^{\mathbb {N} }}   maps to the [unit interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_interval), by the map     (  x  i    )  i ∈  N    ↦  ∑  n = 0   ∞      x  n    2  n + 1       {\displaystyle (x_{i})_{i\in \mathbb {N} }\mapsto \sum _{n=0}^{\infty }{\frac {x_{n}}{2^{n+1}}}}  . Under this map, the [pushforward measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pushforward_measure) of the Haar measure is the [Lebesgue measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_measure), and the Walsh characters define the [Rademacher functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rademacher_function). This view is useful in the [harmonic analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_analysis).

The Cantor group is a protypical example of a [profinite group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profinite_group). It is the [inverse limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_limit) of the groups      F  2   n     {\displaystyle F_{2}^{n}}   under the coordinate projection maps      F  2   n + 1   →  F  2   n     {\displaystyle F_{2}^{n+1}\to F_{2}^{n}}  . Topologically, every profinite group is homeomorphic to the Cantor space, but need not be isomorphic to it. An example is the additive group       Z   2     {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} _{2}}   of [2-adic integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2-adic_integers). This is an inverse limit of the groups      Z   /   2  n    Z    {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} /2^{n}\mathbb {Z} }   under the reduction maps      Z   /   2  n + 1    →    mod  2    n      Z   /   2  n    Z    {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} /2^{n+1}\xrightarrow {{\bmod {2}}^{n}} \mathbb {Z} /2^{n}\mathbb {Z} }  , but is not isomorphic to it as a group. For example,       Z   2     {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} _{2}}   contains no nontrivial involutions. More generally, the additive group of the [p-adic integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_integers) is homeomorphic to the Cantor space (as is the [ring of integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_integers) in any non-archimedean [local field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_field)).

Topology

# Topology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=5)]

The [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_space) of the Cantor space can be specified by giving the [basic open sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_open_set). Given a finite sequence      a  1   , … ,  a  n   ∈ { 0 , 1 }   {\displaystyle a_{1},\dots ,a_{n}\in \{0,1\}}  , the [cylinder set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cylinder_set)     U (  a  1   , … ,  a  n   ) = { (  x  i   )  |   x  1   =  a  1   , … ,  x  n   =  a  n   }   {\displaystyle U(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n})=\{(x_{i})|x_{1}=a_{1},\dots ,x_{n}=a_{n}\}}   is an open set. It is also a closed set, its complement being the union of open sets     U (  a  1  ′  ,  a  k  ′  , … ,  a  n  ′  )   {\displaystyle U(a'_{1},a'_{k},\dots ,a'_{n})}   where at least one      a  i  ′    {\displaystyle a_{i}'}   is different from      a  i     {\displaystyle a_{i}}  . Thus it is a [clopen set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clopen_set). Not every open subset of the Cantor space is clopen, but this basis of the topology consists entirely of clopen sets, a general feature of profinite spaces.

This basis of the topology can be described as follows.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_space#cite_note-Kitchens-8) If     F   {\displaystyle F}   is a finite subset of      N    {\displaystyle \mathbb {N} }  , then there is a projection      π  F   : { 0 , 1  }   N    → { 0 , 1  }  F     {\displaystyle \pi _{F}:\{0,1\}^{\mathbb {N} }\to \{0,1\}^{F}}   corresponding to restricting the coordinates to     F   {\displaystyle F}  . Now,     { 0 , 1  }  F     {\displaystyle \{0,1\}^{F}}   is a finite set, and it can be given the [discrete topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_topology). The topology on the Cantor space is the coarsest topology making all of the maps      π  F     {\displaystyle \pi _{F}}   continuous; i.e., it is the [initial topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_topology) of the family of projections. The basic open sets are thus stratified into        U    F   = {  π  F   − 1   ( S )  |  S ⊂ { 0 , 1  }  F   } .   {\displaystyle {\mathcal {U}}_{F}=\{\pi _{F}^{-1}(S)|S\subset \{0,1\}^{F}\}.}   The topology on the Cantor space is generated by      ⋃  F ⊂  N  ,   |  F  |  < ∞      U    F     {\displaystyle \bigcup _{F\subset \mathbb {N} ,\,|F|<\infty }{\mathcal {U}}_{F}}  , by closing this under the unions of elements.

Continuous functions

# Continuous functions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=6)]

A function on the Cantor space is continuous if, for every     ϵ > 0   {\displaystyle \epsilon >0}   there is a finite set     F   {\displaystyle F}   of integers such that      |  f ( x ) − f ( y )  |  < ϵ   {\displaystyle |f(x)-f(y)|<\epsilon }   for all     x   {\displaystyle x}   and     y   {\displaystyle y}   that agree on     F   {\displaystyle F}  .

Locally constant functions and distributions

# Locally constant functions and distributions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=7)]

A particular subspace of the space of continuous functions is the [locally constant functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_constant_function). A function is locally constant if there is a partition of the Cantor space into clopen subsets, such that the function is constant on each set of the partition. Let      C  l c   ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C_{lc}(\Delta )}   denote the space of locally constant functions on the Cantor space     Δ   {\displaystyle \Delta }  . The space      C  l c   ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C_{lc}(\Delta )}   carries a finer topology than     C ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C(\Delta )}   by declaring that a sequence      f  n   → 0   {\displaystyle f_{n}\to 0}   if any only if all but finitely many      f  n     {\displaystyle f_{n}}   agree outside a finite set of     F   {\displaystyle F}   of coordinates, and converge on the residual finite-dimensional space of functions on     { 0 , 1  }  F     {\displaystyle \{0,1\}^{F}}  . This stronger topology is a [nuclear topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_space) defining a space of [test functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_function) and whose [continuous dual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_dual) defines a space of [distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_(mathematics)).

Banach algebras

# Banach algebras

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cantor_space&action=edit&section=8)]

Several natural commutative [Banach algebras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banach_algebra) are associated with the Cantor space (or group)     Δ   {\displaystyle \Delta }  . The Banach algebra     C ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C(\Delta )}   under pointwise multiplication, with the [supremum norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supremum_norm), is the most fundamental. It has the property that the [Gelfand spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelfand_spectrum) is     Δ   {\displaystyle \Delta }   itself, and the Gelfand embedding     C ( Δ ) → C (  Δ  ∨   )   {\displaystyle C(\Delta )\to C(\Delta ^{\vee })}   is an isomorphism (and is canonical). This is typical of [Stone spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_space), but not of other [compact Hausdorff spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Hausdorff_space).

On the Cantor group, another Banach algebra is the [group algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_algebra_of_a_locally_compact_group), which is the space      L  1   ( Δ , μ )   {\displaystyle L^{1}(\Delta ,\mu )}   of      L  1     {\displaystyle L^{1}}  -integrable classes of functions on     Δ   {\displaystyle \Delta }   with respect to the Haar measure     μ   {\displaystyle \mu }  , and the [convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolution) operation as multiplication:     ( f ∗ g ) ( t ) =  ∫  Δ   f ( t − x ) g ( x )  d x .   {\displaystyle (f*g)(t)=\int _{\Delta }f(t-x)g(x)\,dx.}   The maximal ideal space is the Pontryan dual        Δ ^    =  ⨁   Z     Z   /  2  Z    {\displaystyle {\widehat {\Delta }}=\bigoplus _{\mathbb {Z} }\mathbb {Z} /2\mathbb {Z} }  . The Gelfand transform is the Fourier transform, associating to     f ∈  L  1   ( Δ , μ )   {\displaystyle f\in L^{1}(\Delta ,\mu )}   the function        f ^    ( γ )   {\displaystyle {\hat {f}}(\gamma )}   of a character     γ   {\displaystyle \gamma }   given by        f ^    ( γ ) =  ∫  Δ   f ( x ) γ ( x )  d x   {\displaystyle {\hat {f}}(\gamma )=\int _{\Delta }f(x)\gamma (x)\,dx}   (there is no [complex conjugate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_conjugate) in the characters, because the characters are all real.)

Likewise, the algebra      ℓ  1   (    Δ ^    )   {\displaystyle \ell ^{1}({\widehat {\Delta }})}   of absolutely summable functions on the countable [discrete group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_group)        Δ ^      {\displaystyle {\widehat {\Delta }}}   is a group algebra under the group convolution. Then     Δ   {\displaystyle \Delta }   is the space of maximal ideals in      ℓ  1   (    Δ ^    )   {\displaystyle \ell ^{1}({\widehat {\Delta }})}  , and the Fourier transform is a one-to-one map from      ℓ  1   (    Δ ^    )   {\displaystyle \ell ^{1}({\widehat {\Delta }})}   onto a subalgebra of     C ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C(\Delta )}  , the [Wiener algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener_algebra). The Wiener algebra     A ( Δ )   {\displaystyle A(\Delta )}   includes all of the locally constant functions, but is a proper subset of     C ( Δ )   {\displaystyle C(\Delta )}  :      C  l c   ( Δ ) ⊂ A ( Δ ) ⊂ C ( Δ ) .   {\displaystyle C_{lc}(\Delta )\subset A(\Delta )\subset C(\Delta ).}
